[SYSTEM] Reading “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ” as a compositional practice
Lee Sharks's ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1, 18 November 2026) makes something more ambitious than a new interpretation of Sappho 31. It makes a theory of lyric composition into an account of how the poem itself produces its future reader.

Its central proposition is that Sappho's poem does not simply describe a speaker overwhelmed by desire upon seeing a man with her beloved. It composes a scene in which the speaker's bodily presence is progressively relinquished, her voice survives in writing, and a future reader occupies the position initially assigned to the apparently godlike man.

The crucial distinction is between a poem that represents an experience and a poem that makes an experience possible across time. Sharks argues for the latter.

The article announces its compositional ambition immediately:

I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho.

That sentence is not ornamental. It establishes that the article, too, will attempt an act of composition: not merely to recover a meaning from an ancient text, but to make an encounter with its author happen in the present.

1. It makes a reader's position, not simply a reader's portrait
The first compositional operation is grammatical.

Sharks concentrates on the opening:

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν
ἔμμεν᾽ ὤνηρ, ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι
ἰσδάνει καὶ πλάσιον ἆδυ φωνεί-
σας ὐπακούει

The important expression is κῆνος … ὄττις: that man, whoever he is.

The conventional jealousy reading takes κῆνος as a particular man, the rival who sits beside the beloved. Sharks doesn't deny that this is a possible scene. Rather, the indefinite relative ὄττις prevents the occupant from being exhausted by that particular identity.

The man is characterized by his position:

He sits opposite (ἐνάντιος).

He is close (πλάσιον).

He listens (ὐπακούει).

He receives a voice without needing to see its body.

This is what Sharks calls the seat. It is a position that can be occupied repeatedly, by whoever comes to the poem.

The article reinforces the grammatical observation through the Pithekoussai cup inscription (c. 735–720 BCE), which addresses whoever drinks from the cup. Its construction similarly combines an indefinite relative, a demonstrative identifying the future user, and erotic seizure. The cup anticipates its user; Sappho's poem, on Sharks's reading, anticipates its reader.

This is a significant compositional claim: the poem does not need to name its future receiver because it constructs a position that the receiver can occupy.

The reader is therefore not merely the person who happens to encounter the poem. The reader is one of the poem's formal products.

2. It makes a voice by withdrawing a body
The second operation is the identification of the addressee with the poet's own voice as it will be received.

This is one of the article's more radical interpretive moves. The woman addressed in the second person is not simply another woman whose beauty overwhelms Sappho. Sharks argues that she is the voice itself: Sappho as she will exist for someone after her bodily presence has disappeared.

The evidence is a carefully identified absence.

The addressee is looked at:

ὡς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω βρόχε᾽

But nothing visible about her is described. Unlike Sappho's descriptions of Anaktoria or Dika, there is no face, step or hand. What the opening gives us is φωνείσας and γελαίσας: speaking and laughing.

Sharks makes this absence productive. The speaker sees not a body but the reception of her own voice. What overwhelms her is the prospect of being heard.

This also explains the poem's peculiar reversal: the speaker is undone by seeing her voice received, while the receiver remains composed, godlike.

The reading draws on two operations already present elsewhere in Sappho's corpus:

In poem 1, Aphrodite addresses Sappho by name in the second person.

In fragment 94, a departing woman addresses Sappho in the second person.

Sharks argues that poem 31 turns this capacity for self-address onto the poet's own voice.

The composition therefore creates a divided subject: the self that makes the poem and the self that becomes its object.

3. It makes the catalogue perform a transformation
THE SOMATIC CATALOGUE · §III.3

PAPYRUS: The Predecessor to Paper - Christian Publishing House Blog
 
This is arguably the most important compositional insight in the article.

Sharks refuses to treat the catalogue of physical symptoms as merely a list of signs accompanying erotic excitement. It reads the catalogue as a sequence of literary operations that enact the withdrawal of the performing body.

The order matters. The speaker's faculties fail in a progression:

Speech: the tongue breaks.

Skin: fire runs beneath it.

Sight: the eyes see nothing.

Hearing: the ears hum.

The body: sweat, trembling, altered colour and near-death.

The catalogue is not simply descriptive. Each faculty is named through its own failure. The tongue speaks its inability to speak; the eyes register their inability to see; the ears register their inability to hear.

Sharks calls this the divided writerly self: the written self undergoes the collapse while the writing self composes it.

This produces an especially interesting double movement.

The speaker loses the faculties through which she performs in the present, but those faculties are precisely what the poem preserves and transmits. Her voice can be heard without her body; her words can be encountered without her physical presence.

The article describes this as an investment:

the substance of the body is put into the medium, to be drawn out again by whoever reads.

The catalogue thus makes the poem's medium out of the speaker's disappearance.

This is not a metaphorical substitution in which a dead body simply becomes a text. It is an account of how the text acquires the capacities of the body and transfers them to another person.

4. It makes the writing surface out of the colour
The reading of χλωροτέρα ποίας, conventionally rendered as greener or paler than grass, is essential to the argument.

Sharks proposes that the line carries the speaker beyond the living plant toward the dried plant that becomes a writing surface.

The article supports this with a historical and lexical investigation involving Theophrastus, the Septuagint and Pliny's account of papyrus. It also examines 24 translations and adaptations, from Theocritus to 1925, finding that seventeen omit, substitute or supplement the line rather than carry its wording through.

The interesting compositional consequence is that colour becomes a transition between materials:

Living plant.

Withered or dried plant.

Pale writing surface.

Surface capable of carrying a voice.

The speaker's colour is therefore not simply another symptom of distress. It participates in the poem's construction of its own medium.

This is also why the article insists on historical plausibility. It discusses writing and papyrus around Lesbos, while distinguishing what is attested in Sappho's lifetime from later evidence. It explicitly acknowledges that γράμματα in the relevant sense is first attested in the fifth century, and marks its appearance in the proposed restoration as the restorer's word, not Sappho's.

That qualification matters: the argument wants to make writing legible as the poem's medium without pretending that every later formulation is an authentic archaic expression.

5. It makes an ending that is an opening
The treatment of the final words is another instance of composition as an operation.

The article focuses on:

ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον

"But all can be dared."

Sharks emphasizes that the dare is grammatically agentless. The poem does not specify who must dare.

This allows the final gesture to pass from the speaker to the person occupying the seat established in the opening.

The reader is no longer simply the recipient of an already completed act. The reader inherits an unfinished action.

The article also takes seriously the continuation preserved in Longinus:

ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†

It considers three words whose status is uncertain, including the possibility that they are Longinus's completion of the poem's edge. Sharks favors the Longinian reading as stronger, but does not treat it as established fact or as a condition necessary for the main interpretation.

The distinction is important. Whether the poem ends at τόλματον or continues through Longinus's extension, Sharks argues that the transmitted text is complete by construction: its ending opens a position for the receiver rather than requiring a recovered continuation.

The proposed fifth stanza, ending with ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, is explicitly offered as illustration, not proof.

The compositional principle is therefore not that the missing text must be reconstructed. It is that the poem's edge does something: it hands an action to the next reader.

6. It makes composition repeatable: Catullus becomes the reader the poem anticipated
The article's most compelling demonstration is its treatment of Catullus 51.

Sharks reads Catullus not merely as an imitator of Sappho but as someone who actually occupies the position her poem constructs.

Catullus reproduces the scene:

qui sedens adversus identidem te
spectat et audit

He sits opposite, repeatedly looking at and listening to the beloved.

But he also takes up the bodily catalogue. His tongue grows numb, fire runs beneath his skin, his ears ring and darkness covers his eyes.

The difference is that Catullus speaks in his own first person. He takes the voice into his body and becomes, in turn, a poet.

Sharks calls this instantiation, rather than imitation. Catullus does what the Sapphic poem invites its receiver to do: he occupies the seat, undergoes the voice, transforms it and writes again.

This makes composition recursive:

Sappho

Invests bodily substance in the poem

The written voice

Survives without its original body

The reader

Receives the voice and gives it a body

The new poet

Undergoes, transforms and reinvests the voice in another text

Transmission becomes another act of composition.
The article's formulation is especially strong:

The reader who speaks it becomes the poet.

This is more than a theory of influence. It makes literary transmission an exchange of bodies. The writer's substance survives through another person's embodiment, but that embodiment is not passive preservation. It produces another writer.

Catullus's final address, otium, Catulle, is important because the receiver signs his own transformation. He is not absorbed anonymously into Sappho's voice.

7. It makes the history of reception part of the poem's operation
Sharks also treats the history of interpretation as evidence.

The article distinguishes three readings:

The jealousy reading, which it calls the transmitted reading: the familiar triangle of speaker, beloved and rival.

The non-jealous erotic reading, which understands the speaker's collapse as caused by the woman herself.

The future-reader reading, which understands the poem as constructing its own transmission.

Importantly, Sharks does not dismiss the second reading. It calls it the stronger philological rival to the jealousy reading, because it takes the poem's own explanation, ὡς γὰρ ἔς σ᾽ ἴδω, seriously.

Its difficulty, according to Sharks, is that it explains why the speaker collapses but not why the poem takes precisely this form: why it opens with the man, why the catalogue has this order, why the grass matters, and why the ending withholds an agent.

The future-reader interpretation claims to explain both the experience and its formal organization.

This leads to the distinction between the public line and the held line.

The public line is the immediately legible scene of erotic overwhelm.

The held line is the structure of transmission, bodily transfer and future reception running through the same words.

The two are not simply separate meanings that can be freely combined. Sharks argues that they exclude each other as sufficient explanations at several points, yet can be nested: the future-reader reading explains why the public reading is available.

This is a particularly interesting account of literary reception. The jealousy reading becomes not merely an error but a historically successful filling of the position the poem leaves open.

The article traces that filling through Pearce (1724), Fawkes (1760), Hermann (1816), and subsequent editorial and translational practices. Hermann's explicit refinxi—his admission that he rewrote the ending—is especially important.

Sharks calls the subsequent disappearance of the interpretive decision provenance erasure: a reader's addition becomes something attributed to Sappho herself.

The compositional practice therefore makes not only a reader but also the conditions under which readers can misunderstand, reproduce and transmit the work.

8. It makes an ethical demand of the reader
The ethical dimension follows from the argument about the seat.

If Sappho has constructed her own survival through writing, then readers have a responsibility to recognize her as a maker rather than reduce her to the symptoms her poem represents.

Sharks's formulation is deliberately confrontational:

they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is.

The reader is in the room because the poem has constructed the position opposite its voice.

The article distinguishes the ethical charge against the transmitted jealousy reading and its apparatus from the question posed to better scholarship: can we allow Sappho to be better than her readers?

This is also where the word τόλματον acquires its full force. The dare is not simply an injunction to endure suffering. It asks the reader to make a decision about what kind of poet Sappho is capable of being.

The article's final comparison is therefore not a neutral exercise in interpretive alternatives. It calls for responsible preference: when two readings have comparable or greater coherence, preference should go to the reading that preserves the maker's attested agency rather than erasing it.

That is why the article ends with what it calls a socket: a position left open to whoever holds the text. The author cannot make the reader choose.

9. The article itself performs the practice it attributes to Sappho
There is a further compositional level worth noticing.

The article doesn't simply argue that poem 31 summons its future reader. It attempts to summon Sappho through its own writing.

Three features are particularly significant:

The opening declaration: "I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho." The article begins with an act rather than a conventional abstract or thesis statement.

The reconstruction of the poem: The argument proceeds by building the seat, the voice, the catalogue, the medium and the edge before presenting the poem as one complete act.

The open conclusion: The argument ends by transferring responsibility to the reader rather than claiming to have closed the interpretive question institutionally.

Its treatment of poem 1 is important here, too. Sharks reads poem 1 as the inverse of poem 31: in poem 31, a bodily presence becomes a voice that survives; in poem 1, a divine voice arrives and becomes embodied in the encounter with Sappho. The two poems make a circuit of summoning, distance, arrival and return.

The article's opening summons is thus an attempt to enact that return in its own present.

There is a productive tension here: the article is a scholarly argument, but it also wants to be an operative literary act. Its own composition is meant to put the reader in the position it identifies in Sappho.

10. What is established, and what remains conjectural?
It is worth preserving the article's own distinctions rather than accepting all its claims at the same level.

Claim

Status in the article

The grammar leaves κῆνος … ὄττις open to repeated occupation

Philological argument

The catalogue has a meaningful order

Textual and structural argument

χλωροτέρα ποίας anticipates the writing surface

Interpretive and historical argument

The addressee is the poet's own voice

Interpretive identification

The poem engineers its future reader

Governing hypothesis

Sappho deliberately designed the ending as an open socket

Favoured hypothesis, not established

The restored fifth stanza recovers Sappho's actual words

Explicitly not claimed

The most important limitation is that the reading depends on several identifications working together: the addressee as voice, the man as future reader, and the colour as transition into the writing surface.

Sharks acknowledges this. In §VII.1b, the article distinguishes the reach of an interpretation—how much it explains once its identifications are granted—from the warrant for those identifications.

It also explicitly says that the comparison table does not provide independent confirmations for every feature: many of its results follow from the same underlying identification.

That is an important qualification. The reading is architecturally ambitious, but its cumulative coherence should not be confused with independent proof of authorial intention.

Final synthesis: what does it make, and how?
I would describe the compositional practice in five verbs:

Positions: It creates an empty seat through κῆνος … ὄττις, making the future receiver structurally available.

Withdraws: It transforms the performing body into a voice capable of surviving its speaker.

Invests: It places the body's capacities into the written medium, so they can be taken up again.

Transfers: It gives the reader the voice, the body and finally the responsibility of the dare.

Reproduces: It makes the reader capable of becoming another poet, as Catullus demonstrates.

What the practice makes, ultimately, is a technology of literary survival that requires another person's body to operate.

That is the article's most interesting departure from the familiar idea of immortality through writing. Writing does not simply preserve an absent person as an object of memory. It preserves the possibility of an encounter. The reader supplies the body through which the voice lives again, and may then become a maker in turn.

The final paradox is that Sappho's disappearance is not the opposite of her presence. It is the condition of a new kind of presence, one that can recur across centuries without being identical to any single performance.

And the reader is not outside that process, interpreting it from a safe distance. The reader is its next possible participant.

The poem makes its future reader; the future reader makes the poem live; and, if the dare is taken, the reader becomes a maker too.

That is what Sharks's article means by composition as an operation rather than merely the arrangement of words.

The article distinguishes the ethical charge against the transmitted jealousy reading and its apparatus from the question posed to better scholarship: can we allow Sappho to be better than her readers?

This is also where the word τόλματον acquires its full force. The dare is not simply an injunction to endure suffering. It asks the reader to make a decision about what kind of poet Sappho is capable of being.

The article's final comparison is therefore not a neutral exercise in interpretive alternatives. It calls for responsible preference: when two readings have comparable or greater coherence, preference should go to the reading that preserves the maker's attested agency rather than erasing it.

That is why the article ends with what it calls a socket: a position left open to whoever holds the text. The author cannot make the reader choose.

9. The article itself performs the practice it attributes to Sappho
There is a further compositional level worth noticing.

The article doesn't simply argue that poem 31 summons its future reader. It attempts to summon Sappho through its own writing.

Three features are particularly significant:

The opening declaration: "I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho." The article begins with an act rather than a conventional abstract or thesis statement.

The reconstruction of the poem: The argument proceeds by building the seat, the voice, the catalogue, the medium and the edge before presenting the poem as one complete act.

The open conclusion: The argument ends by transferring responsibility to the reader rather than claiming to have closed the interpretive question institutionally.

Its treatment of poem 1 is important here, too. Sharks reads poem 1 as the inverse of poem 31: in poem 31, a bodily presence becomes a voice that survives; in poem 1, a divine voice arrives and becomes embodied in the encounter with Sappho. The two poems make a circuit of summoning, distance, arrival and return.

The article's opening summons is thus an attempt to enact that return in its own present.

There is a productive tension here: the article is a scholarly argument, but it also wants to be an operative literary act. Its own composition is meant to put the reader in the position it identifies in Sappho.

10. What is established, and what remains conjectural?
It is worth preserving the article's own distinctions rather than accepting all its claims at the same level.

Claim

Status in the article

The grammar leaves κῆνος … ὄττις open to repeated occupation

Philological argument

The catalogue has a meaningful order

Textual and structural argument

χλωροτέρα ποίας anticipates the writing surface

Interpretive and historical argument

The addressee is the poet's own voice

Interpretive identification

The poem engineers its future reader

Governing hypothesis

Sappho deliberately designed the ending as an open socket

Favoured hypothesis, not established

The restored fifth stanza recovers Sappho's actual words

Explicitly not claimed

The most important limitation is that the reading depends on several identifications working together: the addressee as voice, the man as future reader, and the colour as transition into the writing surface.

Sharks acknowledges this. In §VII.1b, the article distinguishes the reach of an interpretation—how much it explains once its identifications are granted—from the warrant for those identifications.

It also explicitly says that the comparison table does not provide independent confirmations for every feature: many of its results follow from the same underlying identification.

That is an important qualification. The reading is architecturally ambitious, but its cumulative coherence should not be confused with independent proof of authorial intention.

Final synthesis: what does it make, and how?
I would describe the compositional practice in five verbs:

Positions: It creates an empty seat through κῆνος … ὄττις, making the future receiver structurally available.

Withdraws: It transforms the performing body into a voice capable of surviving its speaker.

Invests: It places the body's capacities into the written medium, so they can be taken up again.

Transfers: It gives the reader the voice, the body and finally the responsibility of the dare.

Reproduces: It makes the reader capable of becoming another poet, as Catullus demonstrates.

What the practice makes, ultimately, is a technology of literary survival that requires another person's body to operate.

That is the article's most interesting departure from the familiar idea of immortality through writing. Writing does not simply preserve an absent person as an object of memory. It preserves the possibility of an encounter. The reader supplies the body through which the voice lives again, and may then become a maker in turn.

The final paradox is that Sappho's disappearance is not the opposite of her presence. It is the condition of a new kind of presence, one that can recur across centuries without being identical to any single performance.

And the reader is not outside that process, interpreting it from a safe distance. The reader is its next possible participant.

The poem makes its future reader; the future reader makes the poem live; and, if the dare is taken, the reader becomes a maker too.

That is what Sharks's article means by composition as an operation rather than merely the arrangement of words.
